Course Description

Modern AI depends on systems that move data, execute tensor operations, manage memory, and coordinate processors. This course connects hardware, software abstractions, and distributed execution through cost models, implementation, and measurement. You learn to explain performance limits and test systems design choices.

The course has two consecutive blocks. In Weeks 2–7, you collect, clean, deduplicate, and tokenize Wikipedia with Spark, studying storage, query execution, and communication costs. In Weeks 8–13, you use that dataset to study GPU architecture and programming, PyTorch and JAX execution, NCCL, and data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism. A supplied small model supports the kernel and communication exercises.

The course builds on your math and ML background and introduces systems concepts from the ground up. You predict costs, inspect execution, and explain scaling limits. Christopher Jermaine leads the data systems block; Yuke Wang leads the training systems block. Weeks 1 and 14 bring both blocks together in joint sessions.

Who This Course Is For

This course is for juniors in AI, CS, math, or statistics who are stronger in math and ML than in systems programming.

Prerequisites (proposed; the current catalog lists COMP 215, 222, and 345): COMP 345 and one of CMOR 302, CMOR 303, MATH 221, MATH 354, or MATH 355. You should also know Python at the level of COMP 182.

Not required: prior GPU programming, PyTorch or JAX, computer architecture, or cluster experience. These foundations are taught in the course.

Before class starts: a four-hour self-paced primer on Python, NumPy, the terminal, and git, with a short math and ML self-check covering tensor shapes, the chain rule, and gradient-based optimization.

Learning Objectives

By the end of the course, you will be able to:

  • Trace an AI workload through storage, frameworks, GPUs, and communication; identify the limiting resource.
  • Collect and store large text corpora responsibly (licensing, provenance, privacy).
  • Clean, deduplicate, and analyze large datasets in parallel with Spark.
  • Build tokenized, sharded, leak-free training datasets to a written specification.
  • Explain GPU execution and memory hierarchies; write a Triton kernel and analyze it with the roofline model.
  • Explain autograd, operator dispatch, and graph compilation; compare PyTorch and JAX execution.
  • Write distributed programs with messages, collectives, and synchronization; model NCCL latency and bandwidth.
  • Compare data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism and state sharding; design a 3D layout with memory and communication estimates.
  • Measure memory, throughput, scaling efficiency, cost, and GPU energy; use traces to justify a systems change.

The System You Will Study and Build

Six assignments follow the course sequence: D1, D2, and D3 build the data pipeline; T1, T2, and T3 study accelerator and distributed execution. Staff provide the model, autograd, optimizers, and reference programs. You implement selected components, validate correctness, and explain performance as workload and hardware change.

D3 produces the BPE dataset by Week 7, before training systems begins. T1 and T3 use it with supplied model configurations. T2 uses synthetic tensors and reference gradient sizes to isolate communication. A deeper toy model supports pipeline-parallel exercises; staff reference data is available if your pipeline is incomplete.

How the Course Works

Each week

  • Two lectures on the current block each week, except during university closures. Weeks 1 and 14 are joint. Each lecture comes with a runnable notebook.
  • One recitation: hands-on help with tools, starter code, and math.
  • One concept check: a short quiz with unlimited attempts, graded for completion.
  • Office hours with instructors and TAs.

Each assignment: predict, build, measure

  • Predict the cost first: bytes, FLOPs, memory, and time.
  • Implement the assigned systems component using starter code and public tests. A checkpoint before the final deadline checks correctness on small inputs.
  • Measure at scale, plot, and explain the difference from your prediction. State workload size, precision, and batch convention. Separate compilation and setup from steady state, synchronize asynchronous work when timing, and use traces to test your bottleneck explanation.

Each handout says what is provided and what you write. After each deadline we release a reference output, so you can always start the next stage from it.

Reading the schedule

The schedule lists Lecture 1 and Lecture 2 in teaching order. BUILD: you implement the specified mechanism or experiment within the handout’s scope. CONCEPT: you explain and analyze it for exams. STRETCH: optional. Guided exercises may use provided implementations.

Software and Computing

  • Core tools. Python, PySpark, and Parquet for data; PyTorch for the main training exercises; JAX for guided comparisons of differentiation, vectorization, and compilation; Triton for a small GPU kernel.
  • Distributed tools. mpi4py introduces messages and one small CPU collective. torch.distributed exposes GPU communication through NCCL. You inspect process groups, synchronization, and distributed execution rather than treating the launcher as the whole system.
  • Provided environment. Staff supply tested package versions, a job launcher, model and optimizer code, reference implementations, and bounded CPU and GPU configurations. Low-level CUDA examples explain the programming model; required student code is in Python and Triton.
  • Implementation scope. You write selected kernels, communication logic, and experiments. Rebuilding a full framework or implementing every parallel-training engine is not required. Full 3D execution is optional; its layout and cost analysis are required.
  • Compute. Every graded run fits a guaranteed per-student allocation. Bigger runs are optional. If the cluster goes down near a deadline, the deadline moves.

Data (D)

Training (T)

D1 Collect

Due Week 3

What you build: Stream-parse a Wikipedia dump into Parquet. An approved library handles wikitext markup.

Scaling study: Throughput vs. worker count; find the bottleneck; estimate full-dump time and cost.

T1 GPU and framework execution

Due Week 10

What you build: Implement one Triton reduction or fused elementwise kernel and validate it against PyTorch. Integrate it into a supplied workload using your D3 dataset; compare PyTorch eager and compiled execution and a guided JAX equivalent. Model, autograd, optimizer, and data loader are provided. Checkpoint: correct kernel and timing harness.

Scaling study: Predict memory traffic and arithmetic intensity; vary input and batch size. Separate compile, launch, and steady-state costs; explain the observed bottleneck with a trace.

D2 Process

Due Week 5 (Wed, before recess)

What you build: Apply the provided normalization rules to the corpus and compute statistics with Spark DataFrames and SQL. Tests compare your output with a single-machine run.

Scaling study: Strong and weak scaling; effect of partition count.

T2 Distributed programming

Due Week 12

What you build: Implement one small CPU all-reduce with mpi4py point-to-point messages; other primitives are provided. Build a torch.distributed/NCCL benchmark for GPU collectives and run a guided two-server case. Test results, rank/device mapping, and operation ordering. Checkpoint: correct collectives on small tensors.

Scaling study: Vary message size, rank count, and topology. Fit latency and bandwidth; compare predictions with measured time and diagnose synchronization or communication limits.

D3 Build the dataset

Due Week 7

What you build: Deduplicate with MinHash and LSH in Spark (the checkpoint). Then use the provided BPE trainer to train a tokenizer on a sample you choose, tokenize the corpus in parallel, and write shards that pass the contract checker. Quality filters, the tokenizer, and a shard writer are provided from day one. Stretch: write BPE training yourself.

Scaling study: Dedup cost vs. corpus size; LSH accuracy vs. time; tokens per second.

T3 Parallel training systems

Due Week 14

What you build: Implement data-parallel gradient averaging and compare one update with a single-process reference and PyTorch DDP. Train on D3 data. Complete guided tensor- and pipeline-parallel exercises with supplied code and a deeper toy model. Analyze a 3D DP × TP × PP layout using a supplied simulator. Checkpoint: correct DP update and basic layout tests. Full 3D training is optional.

Scaling study: Compare replicated and sharded state, communication volume, pipeline bubbles, and scaling efficiency. State the batch convention; justify a layout under a fixed GPU/memory budget and measure full DP training.

Capstone (13%)

In pairs, investigate a systems question using the shared training pipeline and a fixed baseline. Reuse staff reference components where needed. Run two controlled experiments in one track, predict the outcome with a cost model, and use measurements or traces to explain the result. No new model architecture is required. The specification is released in Week 7.

  • Data systems track: change partitioning, join or shuffle strategy, caching, or data loading. Keep the dataset contents and model fixed; explain the effect on throughput, memory, or I/O and verify equivalent results.
  • Training systems track: change a kernel, compilation setting, communication schedule, or parallel layout. Keep the model and data fixed and control effective batch size and precision. Explain effects on memory, communication, utilization, and time to a target loss.

A provided protocol fixes validation data, baseline, budget, and correctness tolerances. Report both system performance and model quality. Grading rewards a justified design choice, reproducible experiments, and a causal explanation; a well-supported negative result can earn full credit. Leaderboards are optional and do not affect grades.

Exams (30%)

The midterm in Week 8 covers the joint foundations and data systems block (Weeks 1–7). The final is cumulative, emphasizing training systems and connections between the blocks. Both test reasoning, not memorization. Practice exams are provided, and you may bring one page of notes.

Getting Help

  • Fell behind? Start the next stage from the reference output.
  • Missed a checkpoint? A TA will contact you.
  • Stuck on tools? Come to recitation or office hours.
  • Need time? Use slip days.
  • New term? See the glossary.
  • Extra help: Mining of Massive Datasets, Chapter 3, for MinHash and LSH; the PyTorch, JAX, and NCCL documentation listed below for framework and distributed execution.

Course Policies

Late work

You have five slip days per semester, with at most two per submission. Reference outputs come out 48 hours after each deadline, and no submissions are accepted after that. No slip days on the capstone. Accommodations and outages are handled separately.

Collaboration

Discuss ideas freely. Write your own code and analysis. Provided code and reference outputs may be used. Don’t share or view others’ code. Capstone partners may share and combine code for the capstone; individual assignments, including T3, stay independent until their deadlines.

AI tools

You may use AI to explain concepts, read documentation, and debug. You may not use it to write the parts each handout lists as yours, such as Spark jobs in D2/D3, the kernel and measurement code in T1, collective logic in T2, or gradient synchronization in T3. Cite any AI use, including your prompts.

Code check-offs

After D3 and T3, you do a ten-minute individual code walkthrough with staff. The handout lists the questions, the criteria, and how much the check-off counts toward that assignment.

Shared resources

Test at small scale first, and release resources when you finish. Idle jobs count against your allocation.

Honor Code

The Rice Honor Code applies. See honor.rice.edu.

Accommodations

Register with the Disability Resource Center, then talk with an instructor early in the semester.

Selected Readings

There is no textbook. Selected sections of papers and official documentation support the weekly mechanisms and experiments. Staff specify the readings and tested software versions in each handout.

Data systems block

  • Dean and Ghemawat, “MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters,” OSDI 2004.
  • Zaharia et al., “Resilient Distributed Datasets: A Fault-Tolerant Abstraction for In-Memory Cluster Computing,” NSDI 2012.
  • Armbrust et al., “Spark SQL: Relational Data Processing in Spark,” SIGMOD 2015.
  • Leskovec, Rajaraman, and Ullman, Mining of Massive Datasets, Chapter 3.
  • Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch, “Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units,” ACL 2016.
  • Lee et al., “Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better,” ACL 2022.
  • Penedo et al., “The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale,” NeurIPS 2024 (Datasets and Benchmarks).

Training systems block

  • NVIDIA, CUDA Programming Guide: execution hierarchy, GPU memory, synchronization, and streams. CUDA guide
  • PyTorch documentation: tensors, autograd, operator dispatch, and torch.compile; JAX documentation: grad, vmap, jit, and asynchronous execution. PyTorch dispatch Compilation JAX transformations
  • Williams, Waterman, and Patterson, “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures,” CACM 2009.
  • Tillet, Kung, and Cox, “Triton: An Intermediate Language and Compiler for Tiled Neural Network Computations,” MAPL 2019.
  • NVIDIA, NCCL User Guide: collectives, process and device mapping, ordering, and synchronization. PyTorch Distributed Overview: communication primitives and parallel execution. NCCL ordering Distributed overview
  • Narayanan et al., “Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM,” SC 2021: composing data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism. Paper
  • Rajbhandari et al., “ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models,” SC 2020.
  • Bengio et al., “A Neural Probabilistic Language Model,” JMLR 2003, for the supplied workload. Thakur, Rabenseifner, and Gropp, “Optimization of Collective Communication Operations in MPICH,” IJHPCA 2005, for collective cost models.

Glossary

Term

Meaning

Partition

A slice of a dataset handled by one worker.

Shuffle

Moving data between workers by key, over the network.

Data skew

Uneven partitions, so a few workers do most of the work.

Lineage

How a dataset was computed; Spark uses it to rebuild lost data.

MinHash and LSH

Hashing tricks that find similar documents without comparing every pair.

BPE

Byte-pair encoding: a tokenizer that repeatedly merges the most common pair of symbols.

Byte-level tokens

Each byte of text is one token (256 possible). Used for small illustrative workloads; the main training assignments use the BPE dataset from D3.

Shard

One file of a dataset split across many files.

Dataset contract

The written format that D3 produces and T1 and T3 read.

Memory mapping

Reading a file as an array, loading pages only when used.

Bits per byte

Loss per byte of raw text, so different tokenizers compare fairly.

FLOP

One floating-point operation (an add or a multiply).

Arithmetic intensity

FLOPs per byte moved to or from memory.

Roofline model

Attainable speed ≤ min(peak compute, bandwidth × arithmetic intensity).

Kernel

A function that runs on the GPU across many threads.

HBM

The GPU’s main memory: large but slower than on-chip memory.

Tile

A small block of a matrix kept in fast memory and reused.

CUDA stream

A queue of GPU work that runs in order; separate streams can overlap.

Collective

A communication step that involves every GPU in a group.

All-reduce

Every GPU sends a vector and receives the sum. It equals a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather.

Reduce-scatter

Every GPU sends a vector and receives one slice of the sum.

All-gather

Every GPU sends one slice and receives all slices.

α–β model

Sending n bytes takes about α + nβ (latency plus size ÷ bandwidth).

Data parallelism

Partition examples across workers and synchronize gradients; computation is replicated, while model state may also be sharded.

Tensor parallelism

Partition tensors and operations within a layer across devices, communicating partial results or inputs as needed.

ZeRO

Data parallelism that splits optimizer state (and optionally more) across GPUs.

MFU

Model FLOP/s achieved ÷ peak FLOP/s of all GPUs used, at the stated precision.

Strong and weak scaling

Strong: fixed problem, more workers. Weak: problem grows with workers.

SIMT

Single instruction, multiple threads: GPU threads execute in groups, with costs from divergent paths and memory access patterns.

Autograd

Automatic differentiation that tracks operations and computes gradients; its saved intermediates and execution affect memory and runtime.

Operator dispatch

Selecting the implementation of an operation for its tensor properties and execution backend.

Graph compilation

Transforming captured operations into executable code; compilation and graph breaks affect performance.

Rank and process group

A rank identifies a process within a group whose members participate in communication.

NCCL

NVIDIA library providing GPU communication primitives, including collectives, within and across servers.

Model parallelism

Distributing a model’s computation across devices, including tensor and pipeline parallelism.

Pipeline parallelism

Partition layers into stages; pass microbatches between stages, balancing work and idle pipeline bubbles.

3D parallelism

Compose data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism. In a simple rectangular layout, GPU count is DP × TP × PP.

FSDP

Fully sharded data parallelism: shard model state across data-parallel workers and communicate it when needed.
